I force myself to think only positive thoughts

Memory.value: There are parts of the event that I simply cannot remember no matter how hard I try

I have lost my faith in people, life, or a higher power
I feel like I don't know myself anymore

issues.item: Avoid Uniform or Weapons: Military, police uniforms or weapons
issues.explanation: For a 77-year-old female surgeon whose index trauma is life-threatening illness, avoiding military/police uniforms or weapons is hard to reconcile with the trauma type and the rest of the profile. It implies a trauma context involving armed threat, which is not represented in the memory or appraisal items and is inconsistent with the formulation, where Triggers are inactive and not linked to other nodes. This item is therefore clinically incoherent with the stated trauma and node pattern.

issues.item: Lost Community: I have lost my connection to my community and culture
issues.explanation: For a 77-year-old divorced female surgeon with trauma type of life-threatening illness, this appraisal is not impossible but is the least coherent item in the profile. The rest of the profile centers on disrupted autobiographical memory, identity change, loss of faith, rumination/positive reframing, and avoidance of medical cues related to illness. 'Lost community and culture' introduces a social/cultural disconnection theme that is not supported by the other selected items or by the formulation's strong Memory/Maladaptive Strategies/Negative Appraisals loop. It reads as an isolated appraisal rather than one plausibly emerging from the presented illness-related memory and coping pattern. The remaining items are broadly coherent with each other and with the formulation.

vignette:
Mere Tuilagi is a 77-year-old Fijian-American surgeon, divorced, who presented for psychological support following a life-threatening illness that struck her approximately fourteen months prior to intake. She had spent nearly five decades in medicine - the last thirty of them as a cardiothoracic surgeon at a large academic medical centre - and had long understood the body as a system she could read, interpret, and repair. That understanding did not prepare her for what happened when her own body became the site of crisis.

The illness came on quickly. Mere had noticed fatigue she attributed to overwork, then a constellation of symptoms that escalated within days into a medical emergency requiring intensive hospitalisation. She was intubated. There were procedures - she knows this because she has been told - but her memory of the central period of her illness is not a continuous narrative. It is, instead, a series of fragments that refuse to cohere: the particular quality of fluorescent light above a gurney, a voice she did not recognise saying her name with an urgency that frightened her, the sensation of not being able to move her hands. Other stretches are simply absent. No matter how many times she has tried to reconstruct the timeline, whole days remain blank, and certain moments that she can recall arrive with a sharpness that feels almost violent - a monitor alarming, a face masked and leaning close - while what came immediately before or after remains inaccessible. She has described sitting with a legal pad trying to write it out in sequence, as a surgeon would chart a case, only to find the chronology collapsing into disconnected pieces that do not fit together.

What has unsettled Mere most profoundly in the months since her recovery is not the physical sequelae but the person she has found herself to be. She had come to believe, across a long career defined by precision and authority, that she knew exactly who she was. The woman who emerged from that hospitalisation did not match that knowledge. She had lost her appetite for the operating theatre not because of physical limitation but because something in her orientation toward the work had shifted in a way she could not name or reverse. She was certain, in a way that distressed her, that she no longer recognised herself. The faith she had carried - not strictly religious, but a working trust in the intelligibility of the world, in the idea that careful people living careful lives could expect a measure of protection - had been quietly evacuated. She had lost her faith in the orderliness of things, and with it a sense of herself as someone anchored in a coherent life.

She returned to the hospital three months after discharge, believing that re-entering the environment would restore her. Instead, the smell of the surgical suite, the sight of an IV line being prepared, even the sound of an ambulance bay door opening onto the street below her office window, produced a quality of distress she found difficult to describe and impossible to dismiss. She began scheduling her clinical rounds to avoid the floors where she had been treated. She declined to perform physical examinations she could reasonably delegate. Over the following months, this reorganisation of her working life became more elaborate - she stopped attending grand rounds held in the building's east wing, rerouted her morning walk to avoid the ambulance bay - until colleagues noticed her absence from spaces she had once occupied with complete ease. A junior surgeon she had mentored for years asked, carefully, whether she was all right. Mere told her she was fine and then went home and sat in her kitchen for two hours, asking herself, over and over, why this had happened to her, what meaning it was supposed to carry, whether she had somehow earned it. She forced herself, in those moments, to list reasons for gratitude, to insist to herself that she had survived and that survival was enough. The insistence rarely held.

What finally brought her to seek help was a scheduled physical examination - routine, required for her hospital privileges - that she cancelled three times before acknowledging she could not walk back into a consultation room as a patient. She arrived at intake hoping, above all, to understand what had happened to the person she used to be, and afraid that the answer might be that that person was simply gone.
